findings.summary: priorities_first's local _critical re-expresses the rule queue_order._precedence already owns (points >= the project's critical level), so the two definitions can drift silently.
findings.text: queue_order._precedence (queue_order.py:356-358) decides criticality as `points is not None and points >= critical`; admission/ordering.py:319-323 decides it again as `points is not None and _critical_level(...) <= points`. Today they agree; a later change to one leaves the pass's hoist and the ordering's rank disagreeing, which is the same class of divergence the blocking finding on the previous head recorded. A single predicate in queue_order exposed to both would remove the risk.
findings.title: the criticality predicate is written twice

findings.summary: runs.py:1414 and the other position readers call admission_order without config_for, so they rank at the shipped 100 while the launch pass ranks at the project's level.
findings.text: The launch path is right: admission/selection.py:393 passes config_for into fair_share_admission_order. The position/preview readers do not — runs.py:1414 (admission_order), dispatching/requests.py:564 (admission_order), queue_view.py:363 and query.py:471 (queued_placements) all take the default None, so _critical_level returns the shipped 100. A project whose flight layer sets queue.critical_priority to 50 would be told its override-50 request sits behind a review while the admit pass launches it first. No effect at the shipped default of 100, so it is recorded rather than held.
findings.title: published queue positions ignore a project's retuned critical level
